'''Daniel Edward Koshland Jr.''' (March 30, 1920{{snds}}July 23, 2007) was an American [[biochemist]]. He reorganized the study of biology at the [[University of California, Berkeley]],  and was the editor of the leading U.S. science journal, ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'', from 1985 to 1995. He was a member of the United States [[National Academy of Sciences]],<ref>{{cite journal |author = Schekman R |title = The nine lives of Daniel E. Koshland Jr. (1920 2007) |journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume = 104 |issue = 37 |pages = 14551–2 |year = 2007 |pmid = 17720803 |doi = 10.1073/pnas.0707644104 |pmc = 1976236 |bibcode = 2007PNAS..10414551S |doi-access = free }}</ref> the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Daniel E. Koshland |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/daniel-e-koshland |access-date=2022-05-02 |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |language=en}}</ref> and the [[American Philosophical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=APS Member History |url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Daniel+E.+Koshland&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced |access-date=2022-05-02 |website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref>

== Early life ==

Koshland was born to a [[American Jews|Jewish]] family, the son of [[Daniel E. Koshland Sr.]] and Eleanor ({{nee|Haas}}), daughter of the Haas family patriarch [[Abraham Haas]].<ref name=BKFellowship>[http://bkfellowships.org/daniel-e-koshland-sr/ Butler Koshland Fellowships: "Daniel E. Koshland Sr.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130323052310/http://bkfellowships.org/daniel-e-koshland-sr/ |date=March 23, 2013 }} retrieved April 21, 2014</ref> His great-grandfather was wool merchant [[Simon Koshland]]. He had two siblings: Frances "Sissy" Koshland Geballe and Phyllis Koshland Friedman.<ref name=BKFellowship /> His father served as [[C.E.O.]] of [[Levi Strauss & Co.]] from 1955 to 1958<ref name=BKFellowship /> and is widely credited with saving the company during the [[Great Depression]].<ref>[http://www.jweekly.com/article/full/33009/daniel-koshland-biologist-and-philanthropist-dies-at-87/ JWeekly: "Daniel Koshland, biologist and philanthropist, dies at 87" by Joe Eskenazi] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140421051431/http://www.jweekly.com/article/full/33009/daniel-koshland-biologist-and-philanthropist-dies-at-87/ |date=April 21, 2014 }} July 27, 2007</ref>

In 1997, Koshland's private fortune, derived from [[Levi Strauss]], put him at 64th on the list of America's wealthiest people.<ref name="LARichest">{{cite news |title = Richest List Has Gates at No. 1, Plus 83 Californians |url = https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1997-sep-29-fi-37381-story.html |access-date = February 23, 2021 |work = Los Angeles Times |date = September 29, 1997 }}</ref> Rather than relying on his fortune, Koshland chose to pursue a career in science.<ref name="Maugh">{{cite news |last1 = Maugh, II |first1 = Thomas H. |title = Daniel Koshland Jr., 87; UC Berkeley molecular biologist |url = http://www.latimes.com/science/la-me-koshland26jul26-story.html |access-date = October 20, 2019|work = Los Angeles Times |date = July 26, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160413135723/http://www.latimes.com/science/la-me-koshland26jul26-story.html|archive-date=April 13, 2016|url-status=live }}</ref> Koshland wrote in an autobiographical article that he decided to become a scientist in the eighth grade after reading two popular books about science, ''Microbe Hunters'' by [[Paul de Kruif]] and ''[[Arrowsmith (novel)|Arrowsmith]]'' by [[Sinclair Lewis]].<ref>{{cite journal |author = Koshland D |title = How to Get Paid for Having Fun |journal = Annu. Rev. Biochem. |volume = 65 |pages = 1–13 |year = 1996 |pmid = 8811172 |doi = 10.1146/annurev.bi.65.070196.000245 |doi-access = free }}</ref>

== Research career ==

Attending [[Phillips Exeter Academy]]<ref>{{cite web |url = http://www.exeter.edu/news_and_events/news_events_958.aspx |title = Phillips Exeter Academy &#124; Dr. Daniel E. Koshland '37 to Receive the John Phillips Award |publisher = Exeter.edu |access-date = October 22, 2013 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20131022053052/http://www.exeter.edu/news_and_events/news_events_958.aspx |archive-date = October 22, 2013 |url-status = dead }}</ref> for high school Koshland then became the third generation of his family to matriculate to the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where  he majored in chemistry.
The next five years, 1941–1946, were spent working with [[Glenn&nbsp;T. Seaborg]] at the University of Chicago on the top-secret [[Manhattan Project]], where his team purified the plutonium that was used to make the atomic bomb at Los Alamos.<ref>{{cite web |url = http://www.laskerfoundation.org/awards/1998_s_presentation.htm |title = Albert Lasker Award for Special Achievement in Medical Science |website = laskerfoundation.org |publisher = The Lasker Foundation |access-date = July 6, 2013 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090106181645/http://www.laskerfoundation.org/awards/1998_s_presentation.htm |archive-date = January 6, 2009 }}</ref>

In 1949, he received his [[Ph.D.]] in [[organic chemistry]] from the [[University of Chicago]].<ref>{{cite news |title = Remembrances: Daniel E. Koshland Jr. (1920–2007) |url = https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB118559171788881054#koshland.html |newspaper = The Wall Street Journal |date = July 28, 2007 |access-date = August 3, 2017 |archive-date = May 6, 2016 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160506034026/http://www.wsj.com/articles/SB118559171788881054#koshland.html |url-status = live }}</ref> His early work was in [[enzyme kinetics]] at [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]], Long Island, and [[Rockefeller University]], New York. This led him to propose the [[Lock and key model|induced fit model]] for [[enzyme catalysis]].<ref>{{cite journal | doi= 10.1021/ja01498a025| title= Competitive Inhibition by Substrate during Enzyme Action. Evidence for the Induced-fit Theory| year= 1960| last1= Thoma| first1= John A.| last2= Koshland| first2= D. E.| journal= Journal of the American Chemical Society| volume= 82| issue= 13| pages= 3329–3333| bibcode= 1960JAChS..82.3329T}}</ref> In the same period he studied the effect of using chemical modification to change the serine residue in the active site of subtilisin to cysteine,<ref>{{cite journal | doi= 10.1073/pnas.56.5.1606| title= The conversion of serine at the active site of subtilisin to cysteine: A "chemical mutation"| year= 1966| last1= Neet| first1= K. E.| last2= Koshland| first2= D. E.| journal= Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences| volume= 56| issue= 5| pages= 1606–1611| pmid= 5230319| pmc= 220044| bibcode= 1966PNAS...56.1606N| doi-access= free}}</ref> (in parallel with a similar experiment done independently and almost simultaneously.<ref>{{cite journal | doi= 10.1021/bi00854a032| title= The Reactivity of Thiol-subtilisin, an Enzyme Containing a Synthetic Functional Group| year= 1967| last1= Polgar| first1= Laszlo| last2= Bender| first2= Myron L.| journal= Biochemistry| volume= 6| issue= 2| pages= 610–620| pmid= 6047645}}</ref> This can be regarded as the first example of an [[artificial enzyme]], though Neet and Koshland did not use that term. A little later Koshland and colleagues introduced the  principal alternative to the [[MWC model|model of Monod, Wyman and Changeux]]<ref>{{cite journal | doi=  10.1016/S0022-2836(65)80285-6| title= On the nature of allosteric transitions: A plausible model| year= 1965| last1= Monod| first1= Jacques| last2= Wyman| first2= Jeffries| last3= Changeux| first3= Jean-Pierre| journal= Journal of Molecular Biology| volume= 12| pages= 88–118| pmid= 14343300}}</ref> to explain protein [[cooperativity]].<ref>{{cite journal | doi= 10.1021/bi00865a047| title= Comparison of Experimental Binding Data and Theoretical Models in Proteins Containing Subunits| year= 1966| last1= Koshland| first1= D. E.| last2= Némethy| first2= G.| last3= Filmer| first3= D.| journal= Biochemistry| volume= 5| issue= 1| pages= 365–385| pmid= 5938952}}</ref>

Later Koshland turned to studying how [[bacteria]] control their movements in [[chemotaxis]].<ref>{{cite journal | doi= 10.1073/pnas.69.9.2509| title= The Gradient-Sensing Mechanism in Bacterial Chemotaxis| year= 1972| last1= MacNab| first1= R. M.| last2= Koshland| first2= D. E.| journal= Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences| volume= 69| issue= 9| pages= 2509–2512| pmid= 4560688| pmc= 426976| bibcode= 1972PNAS...69.2509M| doi-access= free}}</ref>
His laboratory made three major discoveries concerning [[protein phosphorylation]] in bacteria: 
# The first phosphorylated bacterial protein, [[isocitrate dehydrogenase]], was identified.<ref>{{cite journal |title = The reversible phosphorylation of isocitrate dehydrogenase of Salmonella typhimurium |date = October 1, 1982 |doi = 10.1016/0003-9861(82)90321-6 |volume = 218 |issue = 1 |journal = Archives of Biochemistry and Biophysics |pages = 59–67 |pmid = 6756316 |author = Wang JY, Koshland DE }}</ref> 
# It was demonstrated that substituting an aspartate residue for the serine residue that was phosphorylated causes the protein to behave as if it were phosphorylated.<ref>{{cite journal |title = Inactivation of isocitrate dehydrogenase by phosphorylation is mediated by the negative charge of the phosphate |date = 1987|pmid = 3112144 |volume = 262 |issue = 22 |journal = J Biol Chem |pages = 10422–5 |last1 = Thorsness |first1 = P. E. |last2 = Koshland |first2 = D. E. Jr. |doi = 10.1016/S0021-9258(18)60975-5|doi-access = free }}</ref> 
# The [[response regulator]]s in the [[two-component regulatory system]]s were shown to be phosphorylated on an aspartate residue and to be [[protein phosphatases]] with a covalent intermediate.<ref name="Sanders1989">{{cite journal |last1 = Sanders |first1 = DA |last2 = Gillece-Castro |first2 = BL |last3 = Stock |first3 = AM |last4 = Burlingame |first4 = AL |last5 = Koshland |first5 = DE Jr |title = Identification of the site of phosphorylation of the chemotaxis response regulator protein, CheY. |journal = The Journal of Biological Chemistry |date = 1989 |volume = 264 |issue = 36 |pages = 21770–8 |doi = 10.1016/S0021-9258(20)88250-7 |pmid = 2689446 |doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title = Phosphorylation site of NtrC, a protein phosphatase whose covalent intermediate activates transcription |date = 1992 |pmc = 206329 |pmid = 1321122 |volume = 174 |issue = 15 |journal = J Bacteriol |pages = 5117–22 |last1 = Sanders |first1 = D. A. |last2 = Gillece-Castro |first2 = B. L. |last3 = Burlingame |first3 = A. L. |last4 = Koshland |first4 = D. E. Jr. |doi=10.1128/jb.174.15.5117-5122.1992}}</ref>

He spearheaded the reorganization of the biological sciences at Berkeley, merging eleven departments into three.<ref name=Sanders />  In 1992, Koshland Hall was named after him.<ref name="Maugh" /> The building is located next to (and on some floors connected to) Barker Hall.  Koshland Hall houses a number of laboratories in both molecular and cell biology as well as plant and microbial biology.<ref name="KoshlandHall">{{cite web |title = Koshland Hall |url = https://bds.berkeley.edu/koshland |website = University of California, Berkeley |access-date = April 1, 2016 |archive-date = April 13, 2016 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160413162644/https://bds.berkeley.edu/koshland |url-status = live }}</ref>

Koshland served as editor of the journal ''Science'' from 1985 to 1995.<ref name="AAAS">{{cite web |title = Dan Koshland, 1920–2007: In Memoriam |website = Science |date = 2007 |publisher = AAAS |url = http://www.sciencemag.org/site/feature/data/koshland/ |access-date = April 1, 2016 |archive-date = April 12, 2016 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160412103600/http://www.sciencemag.org/site/feature/data/koshland/ |url-status = live }}</ref> His philosophical essay ''[[The Seven Pillars of Life]]'' is frequently cited and discussed in terms of [[Extraterrestrial life|extraterrestrial]] and [[Artificial intelligence|artificial life]] as well as [[life|biological life]].<ref name="Seven">{{cite journal |last1 = Koshland |first1 = D. E. Jr. |title = Special Essay: The Seven Pillars of Life |journal = Science |date = March 22, 2002 |volume = 295 |issue = 5563 |pages = 2215–2216 |doi = 10.1126/science.1068489 |pmid = 11910092 |doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="Moore">{{cite book |last1 = Moore |first1 = David Moore |title = Fungal biology in the origin and emergence of life |date = 2013 |publisher = Cambridge University Press |location = Cambridge, MA |isbn = 978-1-107-65277-4 |page = 105 |url = https://books.google.com/books?id=fB39CK3ze7cC&pg=PA105 |access-date = April 2, 2016 |archive-date = July 29, 2020 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200729230533/https://books.google.com/books?id=fB39CK3ze7cC&pg=PA105 |url-status = live }}</ref>

In 1998, Koshland was awarded the [[Albert Lasker Special Achievement Award]] given by the Lasker Foundation for medical research in the United States.<ref>{{cite web |title = 1998 Albert Lasker Special Achievement Award in Medical Science: Science communication and education |publisher = Albert and Mary Lasker Foundation |url = http://www.laskerfoundation.org/awards/show/science-communication-and-education/ |access-date = April 3, 2016 |archive-date = April 25, 2016 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160425222849/http://www.laskerfoundation.org/awards/show/science-communication-and-education/ |url-status = live }}</ref> In 2008, the award was renamed the Lasker-Koshland Special Achievement Award in Medical Science in honor of Koshland.<ref>{{cite news 
 |title=Discoverers of Small Regulatory RNAs and Cholesterol-Lowering Drugs to Receive Lasker Awards for Medical Research 
 |publisher=MarketWatch 
 |date=September 13, 2008 
 |url=http://www.marketwatch.com/news/story/discoverers-small-regulatory-rnas-cholesterol-lowering/story.aspx?guid={5544A480-4784-4606-9004-03103E5083E3}&dist=hppr 
 |access-date=September 16, 2008 
 |url-status=dead 
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080919020031/http://www.marketwatch.com/news/story/discoverers-small-regulatory-rnas-cholesterol-lowering/story.aspx?guid=%7B5544A480-4784-4606-9004-03103E5083E3%7D&dist=hppr 
 |archive-date=September 19, 2008 
 |df=mdy 
 }}</ref>

== Personal life ==

He was married to [[Marian Koshland]] ({{nee|Elliot}}), a fellow Berkeley professor, from 1946 until her death in 1997. Marian was not Jewish, the daughter of a teacher who had immigrated from [[Denmark]] and a hardware salesman father of Southern Baptist background.<ref name="memoir">{{cite web |last = Guyer |first = Ruth Levy |title = Marian E. Koshland Biographical Memoir |url = http://books.nap.edu/html/biomems/mkoshland.pdf |publisher = National Academy of Sciences |access-date = July 9, 2012 |archive-date = January 9, 2009 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090109034748/http://books.nap.edu/html/biomems/mkoshland.pdf |url-status = live }}</ref> Daniel and Marian had five children: Ellen Koshland, Phyllis "Phylp" Koshland, James Koshland, Gail Koshland, and [[Douglas Koshland]].<ref name="Maugh"/> Koshland's son Douglas is a professor of [[genetics]] at the University of California, Berkeley.<ref name="ASCB2005">{{cite journal |title = ASCB Profile: Douglas Koshland |url = http://www.ascb.org/files/0502profile.pdf |journal = Ascb Newsletter |publisher = American Society for Cell Biology |date = 2005 |pages = 12–13 |access-date = April 1, 2016 |archive-date = January 14, 2017 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20170114060230/http://www.ascb.org/files/0502profile.pdf |url-status = live }}</ref> Daniel Koshland supported the creation of the [[Marian Koshland Science Museum]] by giving a major gift to the National Academy of Sciences in Marian's honor.<ref name="Maugh" />

After his wife's death in 1997 he reconnected with onetime Berkeley classmate Yvonne Cyr San Jule and they were married in [[Lafayette, California|Lafayette]] on August 17, 2000.<ref name="Tjian">{{cite journal |last1 = Tjian |first1 = Robert |title = Daniel E. Koshland Jr. 1920–2007 |journal = Cell |date = August 2007 |volume = 130 |issue = 4 |pages = 579–580 |doi = 10.1016/j.cell.2007.08.011 |pmid = 17915359 |s2cid = 29934663 |url = https://www.haverford.edu/sites/default/files/Center/KINSC/Daniel-Koshland-bio.pdf |access-date = April 1, 2016 |archive-date = September 17, 2015 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150917193016/https://www.haverford.edu/sites/default/files/Center/KINSC/Daniel-Koshland-bio.pdf |url-status = live |doi-access = free }}</ref> San Jule had four children from previous marriages: conductor [[Christopher Keene]], Philip Keene, [[Elodie Keene]], and Tamsen ({{née|San Jule}}) Calhoon.<ref name=Sanders>{{cite web |url = http://www.berkeley.edu/news/media/releases/2007/07/24_koshland.shtml |title = Eminent biochemist Daniel Koshland has died |last = Sanders |first = Robert |date = July 24, 2007 |website = berkeley.edu |publisher = University of California, Berkeley |access-date = July 6, 2013 |archive-date = May 6, 2017 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20170506070248/http://www.berkeley.edu/news/media/releases/2007/07/24_koshland.shtml |url-status = live }}</ref> A biographical memoir on Koshland by [[David Sanders (biologist)|David Sanders]] has been published by the United States [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web| title=Daniel E. Koshland Jr. | url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Koshland-Daniel-E.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250131034306/https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Koshland-Daniel-E.pdf | archive-date=2025-01-31}}</ref>

Koshland died in Walnut Creek, California, in 2007, after having experienced a massive stroke.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://newsarchive.berkeley.edu/news/media/releases/2007/07/24_koshland.shtml|title=07.24.2007 - Eminent biochemist Daniel Koshland has died|website=newsarchive.berkeley.edu}}</ref>
